utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. And, again, welcome, Ms. Lindsay, to this hearing. We have a delayed start because of technical problems we are facing -- were facing today. We hope that for the convenience of both parties these problems will be solved. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. While the witness is being brought in, we have some translations that have come in and I'll just put those on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And P2131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you should check the record if everything is recorded correctly. Thank you very much for that. These exhibits will now be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, welcome back to the courtroom again. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir is now commencing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everybody here, and I wish for this day of the trial and the whole trial to end in accordance with God's will and not my will. I would like particularly like to greet Ms. Lindsay and Momir Nikolic, the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, bearing in mind that you and I speak the same language, I would like to ask you to watch the transcript in front of you which goes out in English and then when it stops, only then should we start speaking. That way we are not going to make problems for the transcribers. Thank you. First of all, I would like to take a look at your statement. It is Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter 7274.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 7274, please. I'm interested in page 3, line 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we have it. And we see that in line 5, the investigator asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, because there are a number of statements that Mr. Nikolic has provided over the years, this is from 15 December 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer. He knows more precisely the exact date. This is a document we received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the investigator is asking you here what was the basis for the conflict between the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and others who lived in that area, and who filled the reserve force. So can you explain to the Trial Chamber how it came about that the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and then in the area where you worked, and in the place where you worked, and especially in Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to greet you, General. I'm going to answer this question. This is my statement from 1999. This is the first statement that I gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, or, more specifically, the Prosecutor's office, and it was given in Banja Luka. If you have some specific questions about this statement, I can answer them. But you now asked me how it came about that the conflict broke out in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in my area. I would like to ask you one thing. I would like to talk about things that are very familiar to me, and this is the Bratunac municipality, Srebrenica, and the area where I lived. So I know generally how the political and the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina started, but I took no part in the politics, and I think that there are more competent people to testify about that. In my municipality, where I was born, and where I lived, and that is the Bratunac municipality, there were mostly Serbs and Muslims who lived there. As far as I remember the ethnic composition, there were also people who declared themselves as others in Bratunac, and there was between 2 and 3 per cent of them. The relations between the Serbs and Muslims, and I don't know the exact percentages, but I think that there was about 45 per cent of Serbs, around 52 or 53 per cent of Muslims, and 2 or 3 per cent of others. There were very few Croats in Bratunac. Maybe ten people, or two or three families. The conflict in Bratunac officially began before the multi-party elections. As far as I know, in that period, in Bratunac, and by this I mean before the conflict broke out, if we are talking about the political life, there were two main political parties. And it was the Party of Democratic Action, or SDA, which was almost 100 percent Muslim, and SDS, the political party which was almost 100 per cent Serb. What I know is that in Bratunac, both Serbs and Muslims were saying that they are not classical political parties but political movements, and that this was all about life and death. Every Serb was supposed to join SDS and every Muslim was supposed to join the SDA. I have to say one more thing. What I know is the following: The previous system was blamed for everything, the Communists were the guilty party for everything that went bad before. After the multi-party elections, the first problem arose, and that was that the authorities could not be formed. They couldn't agree on the composition of the authorities. The winners in the multi-party elections were, logically, the members of the SDA and the members of SDS. Now, I'm not quite sure, so I'm not going to claim anything about it, I don't know whether there was some other political option present at the time, such as radicals or somebody else, but it is also not that important. So there were various conflicts, and they claimed that they were representing their own national interests. And that is why there were conflicts, and that is why there was -- the idea to divide the power in the Bratunac -- Bratunac municipality. When I say "they," I mean members of the political parties. They divided the Bratunac municipality. When I say "divide", of course, they couldn't practically divide it in territorial sense. If there was a village where both Muslims and Serbs lived, they couldn't move and transfer people. But we can say that in principle there where Serbs were in -- in majority, they would proclaim Serb municipality of Bratunac, and where Muslims were in majority, they would proclaim Muslim municipality. So based on the election results, they also attempted to form the executive authorities. I remember that when the election results were recognised they formed the Assembly and the Assembly was also divided along the same lines, just like everything else. Which means that Muslims formed one block and Serbs formed the other block. Now I remember other things as well. I don't know exactly when something happened. Don't ask me about dates. That's something I don't know about. The police station was also divided, so that within one building, the public security station in Bratunac, they formed a police consisting of the Serbs, and on the other side, a police consisting of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave us the basis for understanding of the structure of the power in Srebrenica and the region where you lived. Can you tell us, was it possible for the war to break out only based on the relations in Srebrenica between Serb, Muslims and Croats or was the basis for the war something else? Was the basis for the war the issue of remaining in Yugoslavia or seceding from Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I can state my opinion about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But give us a brief account of the facts and what was the basis for the conflicts in Bosnia in general, including Srebrenica, because Srebrenica alone couldn't be the trigger for the war in Bosnia. The Trial Chamber has heard many stories from witnesses who have been here before, but I would like to hear your account, because you are best qualified to speak about it because you also have a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Then I will say that in my opinion, the reason for the conflicts in Bosnia in -- generally were different attitudes towards the state in which to live. The Serbs, and now I repeat that I only speak about what I know, the Serbs, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina including Bratunac and that region, wanted to remain in one state, namely, Yugoslavia, or whatever remained of Yugoslavia. But, in principle, it was Yugoslavia. The Muslims, as far as I remember, demanded an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was -- which would not be part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask questions and you will have time to answer them all and say everything you want. And since all these things happened, please tell the Trial Chamber which state, internationally recognised state, existed in Bosnia before the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a republic, part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you about a state, not about republics. So which internationally recognised state existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- you are an expert in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not an expert in these matters, but I know that Yugoslavia was a state in which all peoples lived before the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the conflicts begin after the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia or before? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the conflicts began after a series of decisions taken by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us roughly when it broke loose from Yugoslavia and when it seceded from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the state that existed then and that you and I had to defend under its constitution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But it was after a session in Sarajevo when the Serbs were voted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it in April? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did the peoples in the former SFRY live harmoniously and were the reasons for the conflict brought in from outside to break up that Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It is difficult for the recorder and the interpreters. Please wait until you see that the transcript stops and the same is valid for you, Mr. Tolimir. You were overlapping. Please now provide Mr. Tolimir with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I did it unconsciously. I'll try to proceed in line with your instructions. Mr. Tolimir, would you be so kind as to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked whether the conflicts between the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina come about because of interethnic problems and their mutual relations or were they generated outside and imported? Were Muslims and Serbs previously able to live alongside each other and what was it that really triggered the conflicts? Was it external influence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on my knowledge of the overall situation, I would say that the Serbs, Muslims and everybody else who lived in the old state of Yugoslavia were able to continue living together in that same Yugoslavia. The breakup of Yugoslavia is a consequence of the wish and the engagement of somebody outside of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you worked at the Secretariat for All People's Defence before the war, as you said, tell us, did the Muslim conscripts from Bosnia-Herzegovina go to serve their compulsory military service in Croatia and were they deployed into units in the territory of Croatia which was at war with the Yugoslav People's Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like to correct you in this part for the sake of the facts. I did not work for the Secretariat of All People's Defence before the war. I worked at the TO staff. But my answer is: In the former Yugoslavia, everybody, that is, members of all ethnicities, from my town and my area did serve in units in Croatia, Slovenia. They served -- they did their military service there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war in Croatia, because the Croatia also waged war for cessation from Yugoslavia, were there military conscripts from all of Bosnia-Herzegovina in JNA units in various garrisons from Slovenia, all the way down to Macedonia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we reached the time when UNPROFOR and the monitors monitored the truce in Croatia. Do you remember where its headquarters was and what was the starting point of their missions to Croatia during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And I believe that I didn't really understand you fully. If you're asking me about the deployment of UNPROFOR forces, I really don't know where they were or where their headquarters were. I probably knew at the time, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I probably didn't put my question clearly enough. Do you remember whether UNPROFOR was deployed during the war in Croatia and Bosnia, namely, Sarajevo, and whether they were also present in Belgrade, and did they use these two destinations for the theatres of war near them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that UNPROFOR, at the time, was deployed in these towns and that from those centres it was -- it carried out its activities that -- for which it had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, since you know that UNPROFOR was active in both Sarajevo and Belgrade to go to the theatre of war in Vukovar, and other places in Croatia that were near Bosnia, do you know when the activity of UNPROFOR in peacekeeping missions in Bosnia and Herzegovina stopped and when they left Bosnia and why?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates, nor the time-period when their active ceased and when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if UNPROFOR immediately left Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war in Croatia had stopped and when Croatia was recognised by some EU countries?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how come that Bosnia-Herzegovina could be a host for UNPROFOR that went on peacekeeping missions to Croatia where there was a war going on in that country and that area turned into theatre of war itself? I mean, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I can only speculate about these things you are mentioning. Why, for what reason, I really don't know. I never dealt with these matters myself. I never analysed the situation. I only saw it on television. I wasn't involved in any way, and I wasn't politically active to be present anywhere where there was discussion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you worked at the TO staff, do you remember whether Stipe Mesic was president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the conflicts in Croatia while Croatia was waging war for secession from that same Yugoslavia where he was president? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, Mr. Mesic was president of the Presidency in Belgrade at the time-period you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he also imposed as president at a time when his republic was waging war for secession from that same country in which he was president? Was he imposed upon the others and what do you know about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he -- anything was imposed, I don't know. But I know the following facts: That the members of the Presidency rotated in their positions. That's what I know as a common citizen. And at that period, in that time-period, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it was Mr. Mesic's turn to become president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But whether anything was opposed upon anyone else, I really don't know. That's high politics. I don't understand these things. I only understand anything that a viewer of TV would know, and anybody who followed the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you followed these events through the media and since you worked at the TO staff, did you find it strange that only Stipe Mesic remained in Belgrade as president of the Presidency of the SFRY, whereas, all other representatives or members of parliament or deputies from his country had left and his country was at war with Yugoslavia? Did you find that strange? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that period, as a man who followed events and was informed through the media, I did find it strange for a person to be president of the Presidency who represented a state which had broken away from Yugoslavia and where there was a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the interpretation stopped. You are overlapping and violating your own recommendation for the witness. Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you if this set of questions is really helpful for your Defence. The witness stated several times clearly that he was just a layperson in these matters in this political conflict. You can put these questions to every citizen of the former Yugoslavia. Use the witness to the best of your purposes. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the interpreters and to you, once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer another question from this series. Do you happen to remember the words spoken by Mr. Mesic when the war in Croatia ended and when Croatia was recognised and when he left the position of president, he simply walked out before the end of his -- of his term in office? Thank you. Do you remember what he said in rough terms? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I can only paraphrase. I, of course, cannot quote verbatim. As far as I remember, when his term in office expired, he said roughly that he had carried out his task in Belgrade or that he had accomplished his mission or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that we in the armed forces, that is, the army and the TO and so on, found it strange that we were being pushed in a war by those who -- who should have protected the peace until yesterday? Did you find it not strange [as interpreted] too? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into that anymore. Please take a look at page 3, at 65 ter 7274. That's that statement. And take a look at line 18 where you are being asked what your duties were. And you -- your reply is in line 21.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: It's line 25 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Collecting intelligence data on the enemy in accordance with the rule for the intelligence security of the combat activities and the security of my own unit." And then the following question: "So it was a mixture of intelligence and security work." I needn't read it out any longer. I was sure that you remember. So tell us now when this -- when you gave this interview, did you have a feeling that they really didn't believe your words and that your significance in the war was blown out of proportion? Did you -- was that the feeling that you had?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I gave that first statement, I can answer in the affirmative. Yes, I did have the impression that I was expected to know much more than I really do know. However, I can also say the following. I was not prepared to speak about everything I knew when I gave that first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is very important because the Prosecution submitted this document as part of their 65 ter set of documents. So you're free to say whatever you want to say. Let me ask you now, on page 12, line 19 in Serbian, which is page 13 in English. Thank you. Here we see that you say in line 19 in Serbian: "The commander of the unit." And then the Prosecutor: "Anyone else who was entitled to give you instructions about whatever needed to be done?" And you say: "In the area of responsibility of the brigade, not without the knowledge of the commander." And then continue to say -- or rather the Prosecutor: "You say without the knowledge of the commander. Does that mean that someone could task you after informing the commander?" And so on. And on page 14 in English and page 13 in Serbian, can we please see it, you say. You say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir. I have to stop you. The interpretation stopped because you were reading too fast, and the interpreters didn't find the relevant part of this document. Could you please indicate where you are reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, I apologise. I'm reading from the Serbian, page 13, lines 21 and 22, and the English, page 14, line 21 and 22 and I quote. "I assumed that all the orders are going through the command line." Thank you. End of quote. And then we go on to page 14 in the Serbian language, and page 16 in the English language. And there, on lines 20, 21, and 22, you say, and I quote: "As far as the orders go, I said that as a rule, the orders went along the command line, and this is something that only the commander of the unit has the right to do." And then in line 24 you say: "The commander is responsible for all the units and nobody has the right in any of the units, none of the officers has the right to provide information to anybody, either in a written form or in a verbal form, either over the telephone without the commander's approval," and so on and so forth. In all of those lines, all the way up to page 24 in English, this is where you are answering questions and you're trying to convince the Prosecution that only the commanders had that right. My question is this: During the interviews that you gave or before you came here, did you have an impression that nobody believed that you -- did you not have the right of command, either before the war, during the war, or after the war and that you had to act in keeping with the rules and regulations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this was really a compound question. You have read from so many different parts of this document, it was very difficult to follow. I would like to ask the witness if he is able to answer the question the -- the -- Mr. Tolimir has put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, I believe that I have understood your question, and I will answer in the following way. When I provided those statements, when I was interviewed, on all occasions, before and now, I claim, and I still think that nobody but the commander had the right to issue any orders. In other words, a commander is an officer who has the express authority over the control and the command of all units within the zone of responsibility. In my interviews with the Prosecutors, if that is what you asked me, every time when I spoke to the Prosecutor, I said that I knew who had the right of command and control, that command and control, and everything that constitutes the function of command and control, are within the purview of the commander. I thought that at that time and that's what I said to the Prosecutor, and I still think that. However, let me just explain that I was not sufficiently immersed in the discussions about control and command. I therefore wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how certain things are defined. I dealt with my own area of responsibility, which was intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see D148. Bullet point 115. Let's see what the authorities of the brigade commander are. Which was -- will also show us what the authorities of the others in the brigade are. In that, we have to bear in mind the position of this witness as well. Thank you. I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, you have used the OTP statement with the witness, 1999, 65 ter 7274. Are you going to use it again? Are you tendering it? What is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness said that he had an opinion and the position about that statement. I will leave it until later, after we have heard all the witness's answers. I don't know whether the Prosecutor will want to tender it into evidence. I will defer my decision until I -- the moment I have heard all the answers by this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. That's all I wanted to know. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now can we see in front of us bullet point 115, where it says that the brigade commander and this is bold, and then I would like to read the rest of this bullet point. "The brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units. He bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade command and subordinate commands, for the state of morale, for security and combat readiness, for training, and for the proper performance of tasks. The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfilment, and demands their strict execution regardless of difficulties that arise during their execution." My question based on this is as follows. Did all of you in the brigade know that only the commander had the right to issue valid decisions tied to the performance of any task during the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I knew. I was aware of the contents of this bullet point 115. I knew that the commander was authorised to make and issue decisions and that he was in charge of the unit of which he was in command, and I suppose that all my other colleagues, officers, were equally aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at bullet point 116. In your examination-in-chief, you answered to Mr. Thayer's questions. You said that the chief could also issue orders. And now let's look at the bullet point 116: "The staff is the main organ of the brigade command, and it functionally links and integrates the operations of all command organs. "The Chief of Staff directs the work of the staff. He is also the deputy commander of the brigade. The Chief of Staff, in accordance with the commander's decisions, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates." And I would like to end the quote here. My question is this: Does it arise from these two bullet points that only the commander and Chief of Staff in peacetime and in wartime have the right to issue orders to all individuals in the staff and in the brigade, because this is the brigade's regulation. This is the regulation of mountain, infantry, and light brigade. Please, was that the case in your brigade as well, that only the commanders and Chiefs of Staff were in a position to issue orders, them and nobody else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, as far as I know, that was common practice. In other words, the commander was the one who issued orders, and the Chief of Staff was the person who could be authorised by the commander or in his absence to command and control the units in the brigade and give them tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, let's look at the duties of the intelligence organ, and we will find it -- this in bullet point 118.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page both in the Serbian version as well as in the English version. And let's display bullet point 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see bullet point 118, where it says and I quote: "The intelligence organ is responsible for and organises intelligence support for combat actions. It provides expert direction for the intelligence activities of intelligence and security organs of subordinate units. It continuously monitors and assesses the enemy and reports the enemy's condition to everybody concerned in the command. It suggests to the commander and Chief of Staff the procedure and resources for intelligence support for the brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading. The interpreters can't follow. Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MR. TOLIMIR [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "It provides expert direction for the intelligence activities of intelligence and security organs of subordinate units." I do not wish to go on reading from bullet point 118. It's self-explanatory. We, as soldiers, cannot add anything to it or take anything away from it. My question is this: In the brigade command, were you only the organiser of the professional work of your intelligence service? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, in my brigade, I worked in compliance with this instruction, and I believe that in all of my testimony so far I have spoken about my obligations arising from the intelligence support of the unit. However, I can't agree with you that those were the only tasks that I had. In other words, I had other tasks as well, and those were given to me by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. We will now look at those things that you did as a security organ. We have covered your intelligence duties, but let's see what you did as a security organ. Let's look at bullet point 122.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the right page, 63 in Serbian, bullet point 122; and the English version, can we also display bullet point 122. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please read very slowly. Please, very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Bullet point 122 of the rules of service in the brigades. I'm reading: "The security organ is a specialized organ of the command which organises, implements measures and procedures of counter-intelligence support. It also participates in recommending, organising, and implementing security and self-protection measures which concern the command and other subjects of self-protection." My question: Were you a specialised organ? Was the person responsible for all those tasks and duties, the commander, and other subjects which you organised and directed in professional and specialised terms? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, this arises from what you have just read. I can only answer in the affirmative and say that I knew, I was aware of the fact that I was a specialised organ, a professional organ, and that I discharged my duties in keeping with the rules that I had to comply with, and also, in compliance with the orders issued to me by the commander. My -- let me be more precise. Your question was whether I was aware that the commander was responsible. I would like to say that it is only self-understandable that everything that is done in any of the sectors, that all the activities are carried out in any of the sectors are within the purview, exclusive purview of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Nikolic, let's look at the second paragraph in the same bullet point, where it says: "In terms of expertise, it directs the work of the intelligence and security organs of subordinate units. It organises and directs their work, provides assistance, and controls their activities in completing counter-intelligence activities and duties." My question is this: Did you have the right only in professional terms to control the work of the intelligence and security organs in the battalions of your brigade? Who were they subordinated to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, I controlled the subordinated organs in professional terms. My subordinates were the assistant battalion commanders of -- in charge of security and intelligence. Along the command line, the intelligence and security organs in the battalions were subordinated to the battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: When it comes to the structures of the brigade, corps, and the Main Staff, would you say that security intelligence organs were only professional and specialised organs? Did they have the right to command or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all levels, as far as I know, the intelligence and security organs were specialised, professional organs, and both the subordinate and superior commands were supposed to - I'm choosing my words carefully - they were supposed to adopt that attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since yesterday, in cross-examination [as interpreted] - if you remember, okay, if not, I will find the reference number - you said that Colonel Jankovic came and told you that he would take over all the duties concerning UNPROFOR and that you would be carrying out his orders. That's what you said, maybe you misspoke. Maybe you didn't choose your words correctly. However, my question is this: Could any intelligence and security organ, either in the corps or the Main Staff, issue orders to you; or is it the case that all the orders had to come from the commander, who was supposed to direct you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General. In principle, it's the way you have put it, and theoretically, it is like that. That is how the rules and the books put it. But I was speaking about what was happening in practice. I know what should have been done and how things should have functioned. I knew then and I know now. However, I may have chosen too harsh an expression, saying that he came up to me and said, I command. But he came to my office and he said that he had -- he was there upon the authorisation of the Main Staff and that in the coming period he would take over all contacts that I had, and that he was the one who was supposed to be in charge of that, I believe. That's roughly what I said. And I know that, under normal conditions, the intelligence organs or any other professional organs cannot issue any orders, but I cannot rule out the possibility that Mr. Jankovic and, indeed, I suppose that's the way it went, that he was authorised by the Main Staff - I don't know who exactly in the Main Staff - that he could come to my office. So he hadn't come of his own accord, without a plan. But he came because somebody sent him to my office. And I can tell you that I'm a man, an officer, who didn't ask many questions about why anybody had come from a superior command and why he was demanding that something be done. I carried out orders and I -- my feeling was, my attitude was that we were doing the same job. I never wondered why anybody had come from the corps command or from the Main Staff, telling me what should be done, especially not in a situation when an operation was being carried out, and somebody was there from the Main Staff, and General Mladic and the others were there, so I didn't ask such questions. Theoretically, though, whatever you said is something that I know too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that somebody can transgress their authorities, but I want to define how it should have been according to the rules, and then we can discuss what happened in practice, whether somebody did not act in line with these rules and exceed their authority. It is my duty to tell you that on page 51, in lines 1 and 2 of your statement, 65 ter number 7274.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said the following. I quote --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 7274 in e-court. 65 ter 7274, yes, that's correct. That's the statement dated 15 December 1999. Page 51 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it's 47 in Serbian and 51 in English. Thank you. I apologise. In Serbian, it's 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you say in the first two lines: "So during all of that day you were passing communications between Colonel Jankovic and the Drina Corps HQ." And you answered: "Colonel Jankovic, what he wanted to be passed on, he would write in -- write it down with his hand, my task was to take this to the communications centre to be typed and sent to the addressed commands: The Drina Corps command, and the Main Staff," et cetera. My question to you is: Did Colonel Jankovic speak English? And on which day did he come to see you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic, as far as I know, spoke some English, but he didn't speak it well. I was able to see for myself during meetings. And he came to the -- my office at the Bratunac Brigade on the 8th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since he completed a course of English in the JNA and spoke English, was he appointed to maintain contacts with the UNPROFOR during the operation? Did he come to see you earlier?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't speak English and communicated with UNPROFOR and anybody who represented the international community in Srebrenica. Of course, I didn't even know that Colonel Jankovic spoke English until the first meeting on the 11th in the evening hours. Mr. Jankovic tried to interpret then, and then I realized that he spoke some English. But the fact that he spoke English, to my mind, can't have been a reason for him to have talks with UNPROFOR and come to my office and use it all that time, write reports and do everything that I used to do until then. But, certainly, it was a good thing that he knew English, and it was certainly easier on him than on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber who was it in your brigade who was in charge of communication with UNPROFOR so that we know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that I was the liaison officer with everybody on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go about that pursuant to the authorisation issued by your brigade commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My commander authorised me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Mladic, as a commander, have the right to authorise Colonel Jankovic for liaison with UNPROFOR as he thought he spoke English excellently, and that's why he eliminated Petar from the talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General, both you and I know that General Mladic could do whatever he wanted, so I really don't know if General Mladic authorised Colonel Jankovic. But if you're asking me whether he had the right to do so, well, to my mind, he could do whatever he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you whether he could do whatever he pleased. I asked you whether he, as the commander of the Main Staff, had the right to take with him an officer who spoke English to the zone where there was UNPROFOR. I only asked him [as interpreted] whether he had the right to do so, not whether he could do whatever he pleased. This is a court of law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me something that is perfectly clear. General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff and he had the right to take with him whoever he wanted to, including, Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your commander know, and General Zivanovic as your second in command, or your -- yeah, whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat the question. They didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for speaking fast and being too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did General Mladic, General Zivanovic, and General Blagojevic, the commander of your corps, know that it was you in your brigade whose business it was to liaise with UNPROFOR in the Srebrenica demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could they then or did they have the right to reinforce your sector as there were many problems with UNPROFOR during the operations in the direction of the Srebrenica protected zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this document later. Now I would like to see D202 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D202. It's the rule-book on the remit of the commands of army corps in peacetime. And we'll see that these rules apply to both brigades and corps. Since we know that all the regulations prevailing in the brigade and the corps of which Mr. Nikolic was a member have been dealt with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do these regulations apply to all officers in the Main Staff? That was the question asked to you, and you replied in the affirmative. Now let me ask you, whether the decisions on the professional work of the security organs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last sentence of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your question. You should -- could please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to shorten it too, to make it clearer for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do all duties of the security organs in a brigade, in a corps, and in the Main Staff, are they all defined by the regulations on the professional work in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We kindly asked the accused to repeat once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters -- there must be a problem with the interpretation, the communication between you and the interpreters. Again, they asked you to repeat once more, especially at the end of your question. I don't know what happened. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are all security organs at the level of brigades, corps, and Main Staff, are they in the possession of the exclusive right of directing the organs in the -- subordinated professional units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you provide us with an answer. Perhaps you understood the question better than we did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question. I just waited for the cursor to stop moving. I'm looking at the screen. General, sir, I can answer your question. At my level, it worked the way you presented it. I can only suppose that it worked the same way at the level of the corps command and at the Main Staff level, but, of course, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since, during your testimony, there has been discussion of the corps level and the Main Staff level, let us take a look at D202, which we see now. Let's turn to page 3 in Serbian and page 4 in English. That's page 3 in English, and page 4 in Serbian. Sorry, my mistake. We can see it in English now, and we can also see it in Serbian. It says: "Regulations on the responsibilities of the land army corps command in peacetime." We need Article 6. Could we please see it. Thank you. We can see that it says: "The right to command units and institutions of the organic compound of land army corps (hereinafter corps) is under the exclusive responsibility of the commander. Units and institutions outside the corps' organic compound, those temporarily subordinated, are commanded and controlled by the commander only within the limits of the stipulated authorities." And the following paragraph of the same Article reads: "The commander may authorise certain officers from the command to command units and institutions of branches services, but the commander shall continue to bear responsibility for the situation in these units, and for the work of the officers to whom he transferred some of his rights." Here's my question to you: Does -- do these regulations equally apply to the command of the brigade and to the command of your corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the paragraph 2 of Article 6, the commanders of your corps, brigade, or the Main Staff, did they have the right to transfer certain authorities onto the command as well as the specialised organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping what you have just read out, yes, they did have that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I don't have any intention to contradict your opinion. You are telling us what you think, and I don't want to contradict you. I just wanted to show the Trial Chamber the framework within which you worked. This is a Tribunal, nothing else. There's no reason for us to contradict each other in any of the matters. I don't want to contradict you. I'm just quoting from the rules, and I am asking you to share with us your opinion. And now, could we please look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's time for our first break, and after this general remark, I think it's a good occasion to break and to continue after the break. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue. I have to remind both speakers not to overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please, since we still have D202 on the screen, can we please look at Article 9. Could the e-court, please, turn to the page containing Article 9. I would like to read it and then I would like to put a question to the witness based on that Article. Thank you. Can we see the right page in the Serbian language and can we also see the right page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now in the Serbian, we see Article 9, the first paragraph thereof says this: "The commander shall command and control subordinate units and institutions within the scope of the responsibility received. He shall be responsible to his superior for his work and the situation in subordinate units and institutions and for proper and timely execution of work and tasks in the competence of the command organ." My question is this: This is a regulation on the authorities of the land army in peace, and you have heard my quotation. Can you please tell us whether the commander of the Drina Corps as well was also duty-bound to carry out the command duties over his corps as envisaged in Article 9? Was he duty-bound to follow the same principles? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had to work in compliance with regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the e-court now please display bullet point 6 -- or, rather, paragraph 6 of Article 9. These are special provisions. Can you go to the following page in the Serbian version as well as. Now we see bullet point 6 in the Serbian version. I'm reading from it. Now we can see it in English as well. I'm reading. Bullet point 6, and I quote: "Managing the security service, being responsible for the security of the command and subordinate units and institutions and taking measures on the basis of regulations and his responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, since we can see that all of these were the duties of a commander on page 1, we saw the title "special provisions", then a subtitle "commander". And now we can see his special authorities. Was it the case in all units of the VRS that the commander was the one who was authorised to command the security service? Was he also responsible for the security of his units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the existing military regulations and rules that I was familiar with, commanders were duty-bound to command and control security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 16 in Serbian, and page 15 in the English version of the same regulation dealing with the work of security and intelligence organs. Thank you. Thank you. We are looking for page 16. Or, perhaps, maybe we should go in accordance with e-court. It is page 19 in Serbian in e-court, and page 16 in English; again, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see 2.6, security, or rather, organ for intelligence work. We can see it in both versions and I'm going to read what the intelligence organ does. "The organ for intelligence and reconnaissance work is responsible for, under 1, planning, organising and directing intelligence and reconnaissance activities in the corps' zone of responsibility." Bearing this in mind, would you say that the authorities were the same in the responsibility area of the brigade? In other words, did you have the same responsibilities for the brigade within which you operated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the tasks that were regulated by the regulations and rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say under bullet point 2 that the organ for intelligence and reconnaissance work is responsible for organising the collection, processing and studying of intelligence data about foreign armed forces primarily potential aggressors, providing the competent commands with intelligence information and effecting cooperation and so on and so forth. My question is this: Based on bullet point 2 of this regulation, would you say that the intelligence and reconnaissance organ was also in charge of collecting intelligence pertaining to the enemy side or the aggressor side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer in the affirmative. In other words, in my brigade, I was in charge of that. In other words, the focus of my work was gathering intelligence about the activities of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were in charge of intelligence and security, can we look at page 35 in Serbian and page 30 in English so as to see what the -- what were your authorities as a security organ in the brigade? We can see Article 29, both in Serbian and in English. Does it say here, in Article 29, under the title "security organ", that: "The security organ is a specialised organ of the command for organising and implementing security measures and undertaking other specialised work in the field of security ..." Were you authorised only as a specialised organ of the command for organising and implementing security measures and other specialist work within the purview of the activities of the security organ? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that I was a special organised [as interpreted] and that I performed those duties in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we look at Article 29, bullet point 1, 2, 3, 4. I'm just going to read the first sentences from bullet points 1, 2, 3, 4. Article 21 [as interpreted], bullet point 1 says: "Uncovering and preventing intelligence and other subversive activities of foreign intelligence services and hostile Yugoslav immigration." Under 2. Article 29, bullet point 2: "Uncovering and preventing hostile activities of individuals, groups, or organisations against the armed forces ..." Bullet point 3: "Undertaking counter-intelligence measures and activities to protect work, tasks, documents, material, and financial resources ..." Bullet point 4: "Participating in uncovering and preventing serious crimes ..." Based on bullet points 1, 2, 3, and 4, can you say that the -- the security organ also detects and prevents enemy activities undertaken on the part of groups and individuals against the unit that the security organ protects? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we please look at page 30 in Serbian and 31 in English. Article 29, bullet point 9. Could the English version go back to Article 29, bullet point 9. Well, we see it, let it stay like this. And now can now the Serbian version display page 31, bullet point 9 of the same Article, please. Bullet point 9 of Article 29, dealing with the work of the security organ. Thank you. I asked for Article 29 on page 35. I apologise for not having been specific earlier. Page 35 in Serbian. Page 35 in Serbian. I apologise. Apologies to the witness, to the Prosecution, to the Trial Chamber, everybody in the courtroom. Thank you. We can now see page 32. And now can we go to bullet point 9?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be on the next page. It is not necessary to repeat many times the same because the poor interpreters have to interpret everything you are saying. Sometimes just wait until it is on the screen and then you may proceed. I think we have it now on the screen. Put your question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Article 9 -- or bullet point 9 says, and I quote: "Expertly directing security organs and the military police in the corps command and the units and in other JNA units in the zone of responsibility ..." Thank you. My next question is this: Was your only authority to professionally command organs and units in the area of responsibility of your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the zone of responsibility of my brigade, in professional terms, I controlled a military police platoon and security and intelligence organs in the subordinated units in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have just mentioned the military police, and since you discussed the same thing with Mr. Thayer during the examination-in-chief, could the court please produce P1297 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the document we just had on the screen, D202, is not in your list of documents. At least I can't find it. I would like to see the first page to understand what it is about. The first page, please, of D202. Sir, I see on the bottom of the page the date, 1990. And this was a regulation for the General Staff of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct? What you see on the screen now. I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. What I see before me is entitled the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence, so this originates from 1993. The regulations pertaining to the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't understand that. I only see the date, 1990. And the headline: Federal Secretariat for National Defence, General Staff of the SFRY. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was this in place later in the Republic of Serbia, and/or in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and/or the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say anything about this specific document because I never used anything coming from that level. However, I can say something about other documents. Those documents which pertain to my sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm only interested in this document. If you know anything about the validity of this document in the -- in the different republics of the former Yugoslavia after independency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I can only assume, but I -- I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Bearing in mind what the witness has just said, could the Court please display in e-court page 23 of 65 ter 7247 [as interpreted]. That was tendered by the Prosecutor. The relevant page numbers are 23 in English and 25 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, 65 ter 7247 has been admitted as Defence exhibit D193. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can D193 be displayed on the screen. Thank you. Now, what is this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen. Mr. Tolimir asked for page 23 in English and 25 in Serbian. It's the OTP witness statement of the witness Rupert Smith. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have the wrong document on the screen. Mr. Tolimir is going to call out the right number now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we have 65 ter 7274. Page 23 in Serbian, and 25 in English so that we can analyse what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is, again, the OTP interview of the current witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need page 23 in Serbian and 25 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So now we see page 23 in Serbian and 25 in English. In line 9, the Prosecutor asked you: "Are those books published by the VRS or are they old books? Old JNA books?" And then in the following line you say: "Old books, I think old books. The name is "Intelligence Security of Combat Activities." That's the title of the book, I think. And it regulates those relations. This is a book published by the Yugoslav army before the war." Then the Prosecutor says: "Does it have a little red star on the front page?" You answered: "I think, yes." And then in line 20, you say: "I think there were very new rules in any of the areas. Mostly the JNA rules were used. The rules that we inherited stayed like that." And then later on you say: "And those rules were used" -- actually the Prosecutor says: "Those were the rules that were used during the war." And you say: "My experience ...? It depends on the commanding officer -- but I think nothing significant changed in those rules." End quote of what you said to the Prosecutor during that interrogation. My question is: The rules of the SFRY, were they used in the VRS and does that also mean that these particular regulations about the authority of the land army was also used by the VRS, because 1990 is the year before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, what you just quoted relates to the literature and rules on the intelligence security. When I was asked that by the person carrying out that interrogation, I answered that I used the book called: "Intelligence Security of Combat Activities." And I also repeated it here. That's the book that I used. And when I speak about that, I speak about the books from my area of expertise, the books that I knew. And I described that book, "The Intelligence Security of Combat Activities". It has a red star on the front page, and it was published in 1987. Now when you asked me about this particular corps rule, I can tell you that I did not use that. If you asked me, in principle, whether I know which rules were used in the VRS in that period, then my answer is going to be in the affirmative. As far as I know, in my area, in the intelligence and security sector, we used the rules taken over from the former JNA. So there were some new rules and guide-lines and instructions, but in most cases, and as far as I know, in all the sectors and at all the levels, we used the old rules. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we have P1297. P1297 in e-court. That's the rules of service of the military police of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer showed it to you. I would like to read only page 6. Thank you. Now we can see it here this is the introduction, where it says -- actually, can we first wait for the version in English and the appropriate page, of course. Thank you. So I quote the first paragraph of the introduction: "The service regulations of the military police of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia (further referred to as the Regulations) are placed on the provisions of federal laws and other federal regulations, while those regarding the military police in the Territorial Defence are placed on respective laws and other regulations of the republics and ... provinces." My question is: Bearing this in mind, did all the members of the police forces in the territories where this rule was used duty-bound to comply with these regulations, laws, and other legislation on the basis of which this text was written? Or, specifically, you and the military policemen in your brigade, were you duty-bound to work in accordance with these rules about the military police? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were duty-bound to comply with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have -- can we now take a look at the second paragraph where it says: "These regulations regulate: The bases of command and control of the military police of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia armed forces ..." Can you tell us, did these regulations regulate the basis of command and control of the military police in the VRS in accordance with the positive laws? And did the courts apply the same rules and the same laws while performing their duties in disciplinary and criminal proceedings? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is going to follow the reverse sequence, different from your question. Whether the courts applied this, I don't know. Whether the brigade used this rule, yes. My brigade used these regulations and acted in accordance with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The lawyer in your brigade whose name you mentioned the last time you spoke about it, Mr. Celanovic, was he duty-bound to warn all the members of the military police to act in accordance with the regulations and laws, based on which these regulations were written? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zlatan Celanovic was duty-bound but also the commander of their unit was duty-bound to do that. And also I was duty-bound to warn them about it. And also, in the professional aspect of my work I was supposed to train them in the same spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at page 7 in e-court. That's chapter 1, general provisions. Thank you. We can see it now. Can we maybe move the text a little bit so that we can see chapter 1, general provisions. Thank you. And can we also find it in English. It's page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, general provisions. You were shown item 1 and item 2 by the Prosecutor, Mr. Thayer. So I would like you to take a look now at the second paragraph in item 2 which goes as follows. I quote: "Other units of the armed forces may, in accordance with demonstrated need and the decision of the military officer in charge, act together with military police units, in the execution of their tasks within the jurisdiction of the military police, and they need to be prepared to execute such tasks." My question is: Did all the units that you listed yesterday, the units that were in the area of Potocari and the UNPROFOR base there, have the duty to act in accordance with these rules? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer in affirmative with some certainty to the question whether various police forces engaged in Potocari. Police forces from the brigade and other units, whether they were duty-bound to work in accordance with these rules. I can answer in affirmative that all the units were supposed to comply with these rules, but I cannot confirm that other units, units which did not have anything to do with the police work, actually did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That wasn't what I was asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at chapter 9. I think it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, chapter 2 on page 9, item number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move the text so that we can see the right-hand side of the page where it says: "Chapter 2, command and control of the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we have item 12 and item 13 which says that: "The commander commands the military police" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please be patient. You gave the indication, then wait. It takes some time to bring these documents up on the screen. Just wait a moment and then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic we can now see it both in English and Serbian. Item 12 says: "That the officer in charge of the military unit and institution within whose establishment," so on and so forth, "commands and controls the military police." Can you tell us who was that officer in charge, specifically in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, it was the brigade commander, Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take a look at item 13, which goes as follows: "With respect to specialty, the officer in charge of the security body of the unit or institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached controls the military police." My question is: Who was -- who had the competency to control the military police in the professional or specialty aspect, in your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, when we talk about the professional or specialty control over the military police platoon, I can tell that you I was in charge of that. And what was the second part of your question? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The second question was who performed the duty of the security organ in your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I performed the duty of the security organ in my brigade. That is, Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us read the third paragraph in item 13, which goes as follows. I quote: "When controlling a military police unit, the officer in charge of the security body from paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties which the officers of arms services of military units and institutions have in controlling the units of arms and services." Please, does this say that you only had the right to control the military police units in the same way that the officers from arms and services controlled the units within the arms and services? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, did you had any command authority over those units of military police? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the interpretation which said whether I commanded the units. But I have to say here that I did not have the authority to command and control over the military police in my brigade. In this case, the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was exactly my question. I apologise if it was misinterpreted. I wanted to know whether you had that right, and now you told us that you did not have that right. Thank you. Now, let us take a look at chapter 3. That's page 11 in both English and Serbian. Thank you. We have it here in Serbian. That's paragraph 17, item 17. Can we have it in English as well. Thank you. I will quote only a part from the first paragraph: "In accordance with the law and regulations passed on the basis of the law, the military police performs certain security duties for the needs of the JNA, and in wartime also performs security duties for the needs of Territorial Defence, relating to the following," and so on and so forth. My question is: Within the VRS, and in your brigade, did the military police have to work only in accordance with the laws and the regulations enacted on the basis of those laws? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade, and that is the Bratunac -- or, rather, the military police, we worked in accordance with these rules enforced for the military police. As far as I remember, we had no other rule-book or any other rules or regulations, nor do I remember that we used anything else, but I suppose that these rules were in line with the laws and regulations adopted during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see D203.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For you to be able to see it. Thank you. It's about the rules of service of the security organ in the armed forces of the SFRY, and you wanted to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we rotate it in Serbian. Now please scroll left. Thank you. Please show page 5 in Serbian and page 6 in English now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we can see the basic duties of the security organs as set out in these rules of service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll left. And in English, please also display page 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we can now see item 1 in both English and Serbian. I will quote from item 1 of the chapter -- the heading, "The competence of security organs". I quote: "Security organs, as specialist organs of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces, carry out duties of state security that are placed within their competence by the law and regulations issued pursuant to the law, for the purposes of detecting or preventing activities aimed at subverting or disrupting the social order established by the Constitution of," and so on. My question, based on this, is: Do these rules for the competence -- for the security organs define the tasks of these specialist organs of commands, define their duties the same way as the duties that we saw a short while ago in the rules for the brigades? In other words, as a subject matter, namely, the tasks of the security organs, as specialist organs of commands, explained in the same way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I have never compared the language in this -- in these rules with those that applied to the corps command and the command of brigades. But to the extent that I have read this, I believe that these tasks are defined in the same manner in both rule-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Let us go to item 16, which is page 10 in English and page 9 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
