utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see these on the screens. Then we'll see chapter 2, "Management of security organs". Could we please enlarge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 16 reads: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work, while JNA security organs in organisations for NVO are responsible to the competent Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence." Here is my question: Do the rules of service of the security organs lay down, as we have seen in item 16, that the security organs are directly subordinate to the commands of units and institutions? Thank you. And who was it in your particular case, in your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, General, I, as the security organ, or, rather, chief for intelligence and security in my brigade was directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the brigade. In my particular case, Momir Nikolic, as chief as the intelligence and security organ, was subordinate to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see item 22 in both Serbian and English. Let's turn to the appropriate page, which is 11 in English and 9 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see item 22 in Serbian. It is the last on its page. I quote: "The senior officer of a command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces supervises the work of subordinate security organs according to the general regulations unless otherwise determined by these rules for the supervision of certain work by the security organ." Thank you. Here's my question: Under whose authority in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by the interpreters to repeat your question. They didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in item 22, is the supervision of security organs within the remit of the senior officer of a command, unit, institution, or staff; and, in your particular case, who was that senior officer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I see, General, this item clearly stipulates that the supervision is in the remit of the senior officer which in my particular case was the brigade commander. So I can answer affirmatively that, in my case, the brigade commander had the authority to supervise the work of the security organ. In other words, me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to the following page in Serbian, because I'm interested in item 23. The page in English remains the same. Please blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm about to quote from item 23. "An officer of a security organ of a command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provides specialist management for the military police unit. He recommends the use of the military police unit to the senior officer of the command, unit, institution or staff, and he is responsible to him for the state and activity of the unit." Here is my question: Does the rule of service for the security organs in the VRS under which you worked lay down that you supervise military police units of only professionally and that you're responsible to the commander only for the professional aspect of its activity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already answered this question earlier, but now I can confirm that the security organ is duty-bound and has authority to control military police units professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please take a look at paragraph 2 of item 23, which reads: "In managing the military police unit, the security organ officer under paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties as officers of arms and services of commands, units, institutions, and staffs of the armed forces in managing units of the arms and services of those commands, units, institutions or staffs." Here's my question: Did you, as the security organ in your brigade, have the authority to manage military police units professionally the same way as the chiefs of other arms and services had the authority to manage their respective arms or services? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was duty-bound to manage the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this relationship, which is here defined as being the same that prevails in the arms and services, and we have also seen that it is so defined in the rules for the brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the question. The answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Since this rule also applies to security organs in the lowest ranking units of, as well as security organs in brigades, corps and the Main Staff I'm going to read out to you item 57 and ask you to answer my question with regard to that. It's on page 23 of these rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces which -- the page reference is page 23 for both English and Serbian. Actually, in Serbian, it's 16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 23 in English and page 16 in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can see it in both languages. I'm going to quote from item 57 of the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces. "The security administration of the SSNO )hereinafter security administration) performs duties as prescribed by these rules and other regulations. "The security administration provides specialist management for security organs in JNA commands, units and institutions according to the provisions of these rules and organises and directs their work of importance for security." Here's my question: The security administration at the level of the Main Staff, in accordance with these rules which were in force there was it authorised only to be a professional organ in its relationship with the lower-ranking security organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. It is regulated by item 57, and I suppose that they did have such authority and were supposed to act in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Let us now take a look at item 58 in both languages. I quote: "The security administration provides ... security direction and coordination for the work of security organs of the Territorial Defence, relating to counter-intelligence matters and the counter-intelligence protection of members of the armed forces in Territorial Defence Staffs ..." We won't be needing the rest of this. Here's my question: The security administration, was it authorised only to professionally direct and coordinate subordinated units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what you have just read out from this item, it follows that this is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see item 87 in Serbian in English. In Serbian, it's on page 22; and in English, it's on page 31. 87. Item 87. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you something. You know, it's -- you're entitled to put these questions to the witness. On the other hand, you are reading many paragraphs of these regulations and rules. They are already all in evidence. The Chamber is in the position to review them. You can use them with every witness you want. Most of the answers of the witness to these parts of the regulations put to him were: It is what -- what you have read to me. You should consider to shorten this way of putting regulations to the witness. Perhaps there are other matters you could deal with this witness. Just a question if this is a good use of your court time. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This witness was charged with doing many things for which he didn't have authority. I will therefore show what he was authorised to do. But, all right, I will stop quoting. I did that for the sake of the witness and not for my sake, and I did it for the sake of the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness is not tried in this case. He is just a witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I know that I am on trial here. However, the witness was a member of the security organs of the VRS, and now I want to ask him about bullet point 87, which I'm quoting: "Security organs familiarize the competent military officer with the counter-intelligence situation and, on the basis of the conclusions of the evaluation on the item 86, paragraph 1 of these rules, recommend counter-intelligence security ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Nikolic, is this: Did you carry out counter-intelligence security assessment in the area of responsibility of your brigade? If you did, did you inform your commander about your findings; and did you recommend measures to be undertaken in keeping with your authorities and the information that you had gathered? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily and regularly, I carried out my evaluation of threats. I'm not going to be using the terms written in here, and I mean counter-intelligence situation, counter-intelligence security and so on and so forth. What I'm saying is that I monitored the situation on the opposite side. I monitored the activities of the enemy. I assessed the threats to my units, my positions, the territory under control of my unit, and I did that on a daily basis, or whenever I learned something new I would add that to the overall evaluation that I already arrived at. I briefed my commander regularly about any threats coming from the enemy side, and I also proposed measures that should be undertaken in the area of responsibility of the brigade in order to prevent any negative consequences for my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could the Court please produce D148. We will no longer quote from any rules or regulations because this is what we have been asked by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to refer you to something that you said on page 35 about the prisoners of war. Why did you assume the responsibility for prisoners of war, when it says in bullet point 295 whose responsibility that was? Could you please look at bullet point 295 which deals with the responsibility for prisoners of war? Can you answer my question, or maybe you want me to repeat the question. Can we please look at 295 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, you have given the reference, the number of the document. Please give us the reference to the page number in English and in B/C/S. And then wait until we see it on the screen. And then the -- you may put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The page number in English is 79; and in Serbian, it is 122. It is bullet point 295 of the rules of the brigades. And that is also the unit level at which this witness was. And I quote: "Logistics support for prisoners of war includes the provision of necessary supplies and health care. Provision of supplies to the prisoners in prisoner stations and other locations while they are under the jurisdiction of the armed forces is organised by logistics and other organs in units which have captured them. The escort for prisoners of war in camps is organised and implemented by TO staffs in collaboration with social and political associations ..." In accordance with the rules, are prisoners under the authority of logistics organs? And when it comes to security organs, would it be correct that they only provide physical security of the facilities where they are accommodated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, as you can see, and as I can see, bullet point 295 refers to the logistics support for war -- prisoners of war. Any comment on my part is unnecessary. In the -- logistics support for prisoners of war is within the purview of logistics sector. However, anything else, as far as I know, is within the authority of the security organs and police forces. I mean their escort, the imprisonment, security. And if I remember it well, every order defines that task as the tasks of the security and intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does every order also define what is regulated in the rules, that they are within the authority of the logistics organs; whereas, the security organs define their location, and then -- that they then provide security for the location that they had proposed to the commander. They also carry out other tasks during the -- interrogation, for example.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I accept that you are much more familiar with than I am. You're a professional. I am sure you are better versed in all this. I'm just showing you what common practice was and what I know. And that is that besides water and food supply and supply of prisoners of all the other material resources, the logistics organs in my brigade were never in charge of prisoners of war. I don't know whether this is correct or not. In any case, that was common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you as a security organ have enough power to realize all duties concerning prisoners of war without any other assistance from the brigade? When all the other soldiers were deployed pursuant to your commander's orders, did you still have enough power to provide enough security for the prisoners of war and to carry out all the other tasks with this regard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not, especially for such a major operation, during which so many prisoners of war were taken. I could not do anything on my own, not only those things which concerned prisoners of war, but also nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Let us now look, page 40 in Serbian; and page 42 in English. I'm referring to your statement bearing the 65 ter number 7245.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The number is 7274. Thank you, Aleksander. I was mistaken when I quoted the first number. The actual number is 7274. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now we see it, and let's look from line 4 through line 9. Let's see what you say. And you say: "No, that is not so. This is not what I said. I said that the military police is given tasks and it is engaged pursuant to the orders of the brigade commander. The Bratunac Brigade did not have military police platoons. It never had any military police platoons. It only had one platoon. And that was just one platoon with 30 men. 31, or 32. Or 30 people exactly. When the commander decides the use of the police, if he needs expertise, assistance from the chief of security, then he asks for the expert advice as to how things are going to be organised." My question to you is this: So even if the commander had transferred the authority over the prisoners of war onto the military police, did you as a security organ, have any other means at your disposal to still be in charge of those prisoners of war? As a professional organ, as a specialist organ, were you still in charge of those tasks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the commander issued an order and regulated my tasks in relation to the prisoners of war, then I will do what the commander defined in his order. If this is, indeed, what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this. If the commander commands the military police unit, and if he engaged them in providing security for the prisoners of war in Bratunac, whose responsibility is it then? Is it the responsibility of military police; or you, Momir Nikolic, as the specialised professional organ? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, it is the responsibility of the brigade commander. He is responsible for every decision with regard to the use of the military police which includes this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please answer me this: When you provided the statement or, rather, if you want to answer the question, okay. If not, you can say whatever. Why did you accept responsibility for everything that happened to the prisoners of war in Bratunac, in view of the fact that you were just an individual who was tasked with professional and specialised tasks, and you, as an individual, did not have either the physical strength or the logistics support to provide anything for those prisoners. You couldn't guard them yourself, you couldn't supply them with food, water, or anything else. So why did you take all responsibility when providing your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed the part of the responsibility that I thought I had. Because the military police did participate in those tasks, in the tasks that I have already described. As far as the police participation is concerned I assumed the responsibility to the extent to which the military police participated. I also spoke about those situations which involved the military police platoon. Besides the military police platoon, I still believe that I, as the chief of security or rather the chief of security and intelligence sector, I bear part of the responsibility for everything that happened in the area of responsibility of my unit. I'm -- thought that in the past, and I still think that I as a reserve captain could not have a higher level of responsibility than my commander or any of the commanders who were engaged there. However, with regard to what happened in Bratunac and everything else that happened there, I believe that we all take part of the responsibility and that is what I tried to explain in my statement and in my further statement. I wanted to formulate everything that exaggerated my role and things that I did in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. It is your right to answer any way you want. It is your right to take responsibility or part of the responsibility for your brigade or your unit. I only asked you why you did that, since we have just established that was not part of your responsibility. I will not dwell upon that any longer. I would like us to move on to page 54 in the English version of your statement. In Serbian, it is page 49. As soon as we have those pages on the screen, I'm going to allow you to read that part, and then based on that, I'm going to have some questions for you. Let's look at lines 25 and 26, where you say, in line 25: "The military police department, pursuant to the commander of the brigade's order, they were ordered to guard the Dutch battalion soldiers who had surrendered, approximately 30 of them. They were ordered to guard them, as well as their assets." Thank you. And then you explain where other military policemen were deployed, and it's up to the commander to do that. But let me ask you: Why did you guard those 30 members of the Dutch battalion of UNPROFOR that had surrendered? And this is what you stated in here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We provided security for the Dutch battalion soldiers which you can also see in our -- in this statement. Because that's the order we had received from the brigade commander. Initially, they were accommodated in Hotel Fontana and that hotel is in the centre of city and it is not protected in any other way. That's why we provided security for them. And I believe that later on they were moved to another building and that we continued providing security from -- for them even there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us then why did they surrender to the VRS? Because here you say that you secured those 30 soldiers who had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DutchBat soldiers, as far as I know, surrendered during the ongoing operation. By that, I mean the attack on Srebrenica. I spoke to some of the soldiers and officers who had surrendered. They said that they were in a desperate situation. At least those to whom I spoke said that they were caught in a cross-fire between two armies and that they felt threatened where they were, at their check-points, where they used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard other witnesses who testified about their surrender. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, did the VRS force them to surrender; or did they decide to surrender to the VRS of their own free will? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of those DutchBat soldiers crossed over to the Serbian side voluntarily. However, I do have information that on one check-point - I think it was the check-point at Biljak - that had been attacked, taken over by force, and then the soldiers who were found there were transported away. However, I did not contact directly with those soldiers. The soldiers that I spoke with told me that they crossed over to the Serbian side voluntarily because of their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we then say that those 30 soldiers that you mention in your statement crossed to the side of the VRS voluntarily. And how were they treated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that. Most of them did. And I think that they were treated fairly. They were accommodated and given food and cigarettes and everything else that was indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that UNPROFOR considered the treatment of the VRS vis-a-vis the DutchBat soldiers as one of the reasons to begin the air-strikes on Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that is one of the reasons because of which air-strikes were carried out against Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Drina Corps command ever request from you a report about those soldiers who had crossed over to the territory of Republika Srpska? I mean the territory controlled by the VRS, the territory of Republika Srpska, from the protected zone of Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember right now whether the corps command requested me to report on that. But I know that I considered that my regular duty, to report on the DutchBat soldiers. And I did report to the corps command about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, before you move to another document, I think it's time for the second break, and you should use the next document after the break. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have D183. Thank you. All right, now we have D183. Can we zoom in so the witness could read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is a report from your brigade dated the 9th of July. And in it, you report to the Main Staff and your command. I quote: "We hereby inform you that the intervention unit of the Dutch battalion for the protection of the refugee settlement of Slapovici has fled to Serbian territory. This unit was received at the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade command at around 1930 hours. They were interviewed and accommodated at the Fontana hotel." Then you list the soldiers, and say: "The unit was received without their personal weapons. The unit had come in a personnel carrier with weapons mounted onto it. Signature, Chief of the OB organ, Captain Momir Nikolic." My question is: Is this the report that you sent from your brigade to the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff about this activity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any instructions in the brigade command about how to behave with the UNPROFOR personnel and what your attitude towards them was supposed to be? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to this date, the 9th of July, I don't remember receiving any instructions on that day. But I personally knew very well how to treat the members of the international forces in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't remember, let us take a look at D184. After we see that document, I'm going ask you a question based on both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence. I apologise, it is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 9th of July which goes as follows: "We hereby inform you that one UNPROFOR crew composed of eight soldiers and one personnel carrier crossed over to territory under our control. These UNPROFOR members had been stationed at the newly formed check-point in Zeleni Jadar. They crossed over to the Serbian territory in the same sector. Their observation post is called S, Sierra, and was manned by the following soldiers ... " And then you list them. My question is -- could we actually first take a look at the signature block. We can see Momir Nikolic in the signature block. My question is: Did you draft this document and send it to your superior command -- to the superior command of your brigade and to the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, yes. Everything that you asked me about is contained within this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this your document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the masthead. Could we maybe move the document, lower it, so that I can see the masthead. Yes, yes. It says the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade command. It also carries my number and my date [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because the Prosecution and the Defence agree that this document should be used when you come to testify and that you should confirm its authenticity. So that's why I asked you, is this an authentic document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be good if we had this document in its original, handwritten original, written by my hand. But everything points that this is the document that I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe you could ask the Prosecution whether they had the original handwritten version, and maybe they could supply it to you, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to look at a document dated the 9th of July, D41. Thank you. Thank you. Can we zoom in so that the witness can see that this is document from the Main Staff of the VRS sent on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you please take a look at the last paragraph where it says: "In accordance with the order of the President of Republika Srpska, you must issue an order to all combat units participating in combat operations around Srebrenica to offer maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR members and the civilian Muslim population. You must order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so because of strong enemy resistance. Ban the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949." Thank you. My question is: Did you, as the intelligence and security organ of your brigade, receive this document from the corps command? And did you know its contents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, if I understood you correctly, you're asking me now about this specific document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Were the members of your brigade acquainted with the position of the president of the republic about the way that UNPROFOR and the civilian population should be treated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I really can't remember whether this order was presented to the members of my brigade at some official meeting. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D41 -- no, I apologise. This is D41. Can we have D69. D69. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can see the document dated the 8th of July which relates to the way that the VRS is supposed to UNPROFOR. I quote -- Milenko Zivanovic wrote. I quote: "The UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo has filed a protest note with the Main Staff of the VRS over operations against UNPROFOR observation point UNPROFOR map near Zeleni Jadar. They emphasised that their point was captured by artillery and tank action. The Main Staff of the VRS answered that the Drina Corps command had informed it that the Muslims were using six armoured personnel carriers painted white and bearing UNPROFOR markings ... and that the Muslims had started offensive operations from Srebrenica in order to join up the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. "The Main Staff demanded that UNPROFOR warn the Muslim forces to withdraw to within the borders of the demilitarised zones." And then the penultimate paragraph: "The Main Staff has ordered you not to attack UNPROFOR, but to prevent any surprises and stop the Muslims in their intention to join up Srebrenica and Zepa. "Good luck in war and best regards from General Tolimir. "Commander, Major-General Milenko Zivanovic." My question is: Did General Zivanovic write this based on the telegram and information received in the Main Staff and did he send this to the subordinate command, that is, the brigade command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these things you're asking me, I can't answer you. I don't know from whom General Zivanovic received his information. I cannot comment on that. Now whether it arrived my unit, I can just look at what it says here on the list of addressees, and it says IKM of Drina Corps, but, here in the list of addressees, I don't see that it had been sent to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Was the Main Staff supposed to deliver this straight to your brigade and to you personally, or was he supposed to do that through the Drina Corps, and then the Drina Corps was supposed to forward it to the brigades that took part in the action; and can that be deduced from this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, yes, this is a more specific question. This document shows that the Drina Corps command received this document at its forward command post at Pribicevac. It was delivered personally to the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radislav Krstic. He commanded at the time, and he was in the zone of responsibility of, the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Do you see here where it says "to", "also to Major-General Zdravko Tolimir for information." My question is: Is General Zivanovic informing me that that he forwarded the information that I received from UNPROFOR in Sarajevo; and did he, in the last paragraph, even write, "Good luck in war and best regards from General Tolimir." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, could you tell us, do you know that UNPROFOR, in Sarajevo, requested that either Nicolai, deputising for Rupert Smith or Gobillard should arrive at Srebrenica? And do you know that General Mladic approved their arrival on the 11th or on the 12th, and were you informed about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the previous situations that you mentioned. I don't know -- I had no information about anything at that level. But I did know that, on the 11th and 12th, somebody was supposed to come from the main command to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you told that the UNPROFOR commander personally - in this case, General Nicolai as the one who was deputising for the commander in Sarajevo - wanted to see the situation because being a Dutchman, he didn't believe that the Dutch soldiers had surrendered but he believed that we had taken them prisoner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe -- correction, I don't remember that precisely. But I believe that there was doubt expressed with regard to the status of the soldiers in the Bratunac territory. But I don't remember the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at document D64. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a document of the Drina Corps command and its intelligence department, drafted on 12 July 1995, and sent to the intelligence department and the commands of the corps mentioned here, as well as the forward command post, personally to the commander of the staff, General Krstic, as well as to the Bratunac forward command post, to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. In paragraph 2, we read: "On 12 July of this year, at 1945 hours, a radio network of elements of the 28th Muslim Division was activated; during the morning, at around 0500 hours, these elements came across a minefield in the sector of Ravni Buljin at the juncture between the Milic and Bratunac Brigades." And it goes on to say in the following paragraphs where those making up that radio network are situated, are located. And then we see in the fourth paragraph: "Those who communicated over the radio network were extremely frightened and yet undecided about the direction of breaking through the line of defence of the Zvornik Brigade and the 1st Bratunac Infantry Brigade. In addition, it is not clear whether all elements of these units have been pulled out from the area of the former Muslim enclave of Srebrenica since they were discovered in the early morning hours after they had activated our minefield." In the last two lines of this document - could we please scroll down; I'm referring to the page in Serbian - it says: "The Muslims want to present Srebrenica as a demilitarized zone in which there was only civilian population and that is why they ordered all armed and able-bodied persons to illegally pull out through the territory of the RS to the territory controlled by the Muslims so that they could accuse the VRS of an unprovoked attack on civilians in a safe haven." Before the signature block but below the stamp, we see -- or actually let us read the following paragraph: "Although it is very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible, or liquidate them if they resist, it is equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. "The intelligence and security organs will brief the MUP organs in their respective areas of responsibility on information received. They will draw up joint plans from breaking up and liquidating the enemy formations trying to escape from Srebrenica enclave towards Tuzla and Kladanj. "Chief, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir." Here's my question: Did you know that the security administration had this information about the intentions of the Muslims, namely, to pull out from Srebrenica and to make it seem as if the civilian population had been attacked; and was this document drafted on the 12th of July; and was it received in your brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you, in the Main Staff, knew and what kind of information you had, and the same applies to the Drina Corps, I really don't know. I cannot comment on that. I cannot state with full certainty, but I think I have not seen this document before, although I see that my brigade is one of the intended recipients. But I cannot state with any certainty that it arrived or did not arrive. But I don't really remember all its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But, based on the contents, would -- is it necessary for Popovic and Krstic to brief your brigade commander, since this was addressed to the security and intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I have been able to infer from this document during this short time shows that this document should have arrived at the Bratunac Brigade from the Drina Corps, because we see for whom it was intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get any information about the Muslims' intentions to pull out from the enclave, including soldiers and able-bodied men; whereas, women and children were to be transported to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I cannot confirm that this is the exact information we received then. But I can say that our expectations were also that the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the members of the 28th Division at Srebrenica would leave the territory without taking the civilian population with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the brigade did have information that able-bodied Muslim men wanted to break through to the territory controlled by the BH army; whereas, the women and children were to be separately taken to destinations in the territory of the Federation, assisted by UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can put it that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the Prosecutor's document 65 ter number 5908. Thank you. Thank you. The document you want is 65 ter 5908 from e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registry can't find a document under this number. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I know these things happen. If there's another list, an amended list, we'd appreciate it. We've got about four or five documents now that haven't been on the most recent list that we received. So we would appreciate it if there is an amended list. It just helps us with our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. I find myself in the same situation. We received during this session an updated list. But at least six documents are not listed which were used with the witness during today's hearing. And I would like to indicate the numbers: D41, D64, D148, D183, D184, and 65 ter 7274. I don't find these documents on the list of documents to be used with this witness. And please check again the number of the last document you are asking for. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, I will check the matter so that, for the following session, everybody will be provided with a complete list of documents. There seems to have been some minor technical problems. At any rate, I will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are in the -- are you in the fortunate situation that you have several days to update the list. Because the next session will be on Monday. Please check the number you are asking for now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then we will not use this document until it is uploaded to e-court. But as I have referred to it, I want to tell Mr. Nikolic that this is a simple report drafted by him on the 9th of July. It is only five sentences long, about which I wanted to ask him, but then can I do that later. If necessary, we can put it on the ELMO, or use it once it is uploaded to e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's up to you decide if you want to deal with this document now. Then we can put it on the ELMO. If you want to postpone it and deal with that later, it's possible. The court usher will assist you with the document and put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we're speaking about the 9th of July, and this is the topic we're dealing with, it's better to look at it now so as not to go back to it later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem with the ELMO at the moment. I hope it can be resolved. Now we have it. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a document here which was sent from Bratunac on the 9th of July. It was sent by the command of the Bratunac Brigade from the chief of the security and intelligence organ. I quote: "We inform you that the command of the DutchBat requests a meeting with a representative of the Serb side. The request was transferred to the Zuti Most check-point. The liaison officer of DutchBat did not relate the contents of the matter they wished to discuss with the Serb side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just noticed that this document has been used by the Defence as a 1D number and that may be in e-court. And I believe there is a translation, so I think we can get it up on e-court and look at the English as well. And I believe it is 1D00727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Registry will try to call it up on the screen. We have this document in the list of the Defence, but there's a note that the translation is still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I thought there was one available, Mr. President, but apparently it's not -- it's not ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, only briefly, if I may, in order to resolve the problem. Mr. Tolimir read out the 65 ter number of the Prosecution. For some reason, it is not in e-court but we will see to it that a translation becomes available as soon as possible. But I hope that we can still use it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is possible to use it. It is in e-court with number 1D727. Mr. Tolimir, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this has not been translated, can you tell us if this is an original document? It has been taken off the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen because it is in e-court. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the meantime, we have been able to upload this document with a translation under 65 ter 5908. So it is -- I think it's now available under the Prosecution 65 ter number with a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. It is -- the system is improving from minute to minute. Great. Mr. Tolimir, now you can use the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, tell us, please, whether you wrote and signed this document and whether you sent it to the superior commands and corresponding security organs. Can you also explain its contents and tell us why it was that the DutchBat command requested a meeting with you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see it on the screen in front of me. I don't know how it get it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, everything is quite obvious here. This document was drafted in my command. It bears my number and my signature. As for the contents, you can see it for yourself. You can see what I wrote. I don't know the reasons. I don't know why they requested the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the meeting was held; and, if it wasn't, why not? We are talking about the 9th of July here.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no information to the fact -- to the effect that this meeting took place. If it had, I'm sure that I would have drafted a report about it. I don't know if the meeting took place. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know who was the deputy of Mr. Karremans and which function he performed and was his name? Did he ever request to meet you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who was introduced to me and that I consider Karremans' deputy, I think it was Major Boering. I don't know whether I am pronouncing it correctly. He's the officer that used to meet me on a number of occasions. I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, tell us, do you know that the members of the DutchBat in Srebrenica received so-called green alert, which meant that they were supposed to open fire on the members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Green order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, could be more precise about the time-period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether, on the 9th, 10th, and the 11th, the so-called green order was issued to the DutchBat members to engage in combat activities against the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such an order. I have never heard something like that before. This is the first time that I hear it now, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the soldiers who defected to the territory of the Republika Srpska tell you that they were requested to act against the VRS, that the Muslims requested that, and that their command issued such orders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I learned in a conversation with those soldiers, I think that I only had one conversation with them, with one group, I learned that the representatives of the Muslim side insisted that the UNPROFOR forces should, together with them, resist the attack of the Serb forces. I also have the information that the members of the Dutch battalion were threatened with weapons. They were told that they had to take part in that. So that's what I learned from them. Nothing more than that. I don't know what assignments they received from their own command because, in those days, I didn't meet up with anybody, and I did not attend any meeting with the representatives of the DutchBat. My only contact was with those members of the DutchBat who defected to Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to avoid me the beginning of the next topic, because I would have to consult some other documents, I propose that we do that the following day of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. You have used this document we have on the screen now. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We saved this document for this witness, so I would like to tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 5908 shall be assigned Exhibit number D204. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, we have to adjourn for the day and for the week. I -- I'm convinced that you will appreciate to have a rest now after four days of testimony. We adjourn and resume on Monday in the afternoon, 2.15 in this courtroom. And the Chamber would appreciate to receive a complete updated list of documents. That would be helpful. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th of April, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
